---
title: "Power curves: sweeping one parameter at a time"
output: html_document
---

<!--
WHAT A POWER CURVE IS, IN PLAIN TERMS

Right now you run the pipeline once and get one number per method, e.g.
"quasibinomial recall = 0.62". That is one dot.

A power curve is that same dot, computed again and again at different
settings, and joined into a line. x = the setting you varied, y = the
metric, one line per method.

So to draw it you need a table shaped like this, one row per
(setting, seed, method):

   n_reps  seed  method              recall  precision  bal_acc   AUC
   3       1     GLM quasibinomial   0.21    0.94       0.88      0.79
   3       1     Fisher (pooled)     0.55    0.48       0.71      0.81
   5       1     GLM quasibinomial   0.38    0.95       0.90      0.84
   ...

Everything below exists to build that table. The plotting itself is
three lines at the very end.

NEEDS: p, f0 from your main script, and evaluate() / auc() / adj()
from section 5 of the stats file.
-->


```{r libraries}
# ----------------------------------------------------------------
library(A2iSimR, lib.loc = "R_library")
packageVersion("A2iSimR")
library(ggplot2)

```


```{r preparation}
# -----------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. prep everything before creating the pipeline

p <- a2i_calibrated_params("HEK293T__joint_condition_primary")

f0 <- a2i_make_features(p, n_transcripts = 4000, n_sites = 10000, seed = 101)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. SCORE THE METHODS
# ------------------------------------------------------------------

# Multiple testing: you ran thousands of tests, so 5% of null sites would
# hit p < 0.05 by luck alone. Benjamini-Hochberg converts p-values into
# q-values, which you can threshold at 0.05 to target a 5% false
# discovery rate.
# a function to adjust p-values
adj <- function(p) stats::p.adjust(p, method = "BH")

# Area under the ROC curve, computed from ranks (no extra package).
# 1.0 = perfect ranking, 0.5 = coin flip.
# This computes the AUC (area under the ROC curve). First it drops sites where the test produced no p-value (NA), 
# keeping the "true answer" vector aligned.
auc <- function(p, truth) {
  ok <- is.finite(p)
  p <- p[ok]; truth <- truth[ok]
  
  # AUC compares true sites against null sites, so if there are no true sites, 
  # or no null sites, it can't be computed, and it returns NA.
  if (!any(truth) || all(truth)) return(NA_real_)
  
  #The result is the probability that a random true site gets a smaller p-value 
  # than a random null site. 1.0 is perfect, 0.5 is a coin flip.
  score <- -p                       # smaller p = stronger evidence
  r  <- rank(score)                 # rank() averages ties, which is correct
  n1 <- sum(truth); n0 <- sum(!truth)
  (sum(r[truth]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}

# Area under the precision-recall curve (average precision).
# Random ranking gives AUPRC = fraction of true sites, NOT 0.5.
auprc <- function(p, truth) {
  ok <- is.finite(p)
  p <- p[ok]; truth <- truth[ok]
  n1 <- sum(truth)
  if (n1 == 0 || n1 == length(truth)) return(NA_real_)

  o <- order(p)                       # smallest p = strongest evidence first
  p <- p[o]; truth <- truth[o]

  tp <- cumsum(truth)
  fp <- cumsum(!truth)

  # Tied p-values (e.g. many p = 1) must enter together, so only
  # evaluate the curve at the last site of each block of ties.
  last <- c(p[-1] != p[-length(p)], TRUE)
  tp <- tp[last]; fp <- fp[last]

  precision <- tp / (tp + fp)
  recall    <- tp / n1

  sum(diff(c(0, recall)) * precision)
}

# ---- the four metrics -------------------------------------------
#
# Every site falls into one of four boxes once a method has called it:
#
#                        truly differential   truly null
#   called significant          TP                FP
#   not called                  FN                TN
#
#   accuracy  = (TP + TN) / everything
#               "how often was the method right, either way"
#   precision = TP / (TP + FP)
#               "of the sites it called, how many were real"   (= 1 - FDR)
#   recall    = TP / (TP + FN)
#               "of the real sites, how many did it find"      (= power)
#   AUC       = how well the p-values RANK true sites above null ones,
#               across every possible cutoff. It needs no cutoff at all.
#
# accuracy, precision and recall all depend on where you put the cutoff
# (here: BH q < 0.05). AUC does not.

#This function grades one method. ok marks the sites the method could test. 
#q are the BH-adjusted values. hit marks sites called significant. 
#Then it keeps only testable sites for both the truth and the calls, 
#so untestable sites aren't counted as "correctly not called."
evaluate <- function(p, truth, alpha = 0.05) {
  ok    <- is.finite(p)                 # sites the method could actually test
  q     <- adj(p)
  hit   <- ok & is.finite(q) & q < alpha # called significant
  t_ok  <- truth[ok]
  h_ok  <- hit[ok]

  TP <- sum( h_ok &  t_ok)
  FP <- sum( h_ok & !t_ok)
  FN <- sum(!h_ok &  t_ok)
  TN <- sum(!h_ok & !t_ok)

  #Precision is "of what I called, how much was real." 
  #Recall is "of what was real, how much did I find" (this is power). 
  #The if guards avoid dividing by zero, returning NA instead.
  precision <- if (TP + FP > 0) TP / (TP + FP) else NA_real_
  recall    <- if (TP + FN > 0) TP / (TP + FN) else NA_real_

  data.frame(
    tested    = sum(ok),
    called    = TP + FP,
    called_raw = sum(ok & p < alpha),
    accuracy  = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN),
    AUC       = auc(p, truth),
    AUPRC          = auprc(p, truth),
    AUPRC_baseline = mean(truth[ok]),
    precision = precision,
    recall    = recall,
    # F1 is the balance between precision and recall - handy as a single
    # number when one method wins on precision and another on recall.
    F1        = if (is.finite(precision) && is.finite(recall) &&
                    precision + recall > 0) {
                  2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)
                } else NA_real_,
    # balanced accuracy = average of recall and specificity. Plain accuracy
    # is misleading here (see note below); this one is not.
    balanced_accuracy   = mean(c(recall, if (TN + FP > 0) TN / (TN + FP) else NA_real_)),
    TP = TP,
    FP = FP,
    FN = FN,
    TN = TN
  )
}

auprc_baseline <- function(dat, xvar) {
  stopifnot(is.data.frame(dat),
            all(c("method", xvar, "AUPRC_baseline") %in% names(dat)))
  b <- aggregate(dat["AUPRC_baseline"],
                 by = dat[c("method", xvar)], FUN = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
  names(b)[names(b) == "AUPRC_baseline"] <- "value"
  b$metric <- factor("AUPRC",
                     levels = c("recall", "precision", "AUC", "AUPRC", "balanced_accuracy"))
  geom_line(data = b, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.5)
}


```

```{r wrap}
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Wrap the WHOLE pipeline into one function
#
# Every argument has a default equal to your baseline scenario. When you
# sweep one parameter, you pass only that one and the rest stay at
# baseline automatically. That is the answer to "how do I know the
# setting of the parameters I am not testing" - they are written here,
# once, and never move.
# ------------------------------------------------------------------

run_one <- function(n_reps       = 3,     # <- baseline values
                    strength     = 1,
                    target_depth = 100,
                    phi          = 50,
                    seed         = 1,
                    use_fisher   = TRUE) {

  # ---- (a) build the scenario, exactly as in your main script -------
  #This copies the original features
  f <- f0

  # find all the effect-size columns automatically instead of typing out
  # all five names, so this cannot get out of sync
  #finds every column whose name starts with de_logit_shift_condition 
  #(these hold how much editing shifts between conditions at each site) 
  #and multiplies them by strength. So strength = 2 doubles every effect, 
  #0.5 halves it.
  de_cols <- grep("^de_logit_shift_condition", names(f0$site_info), value = TRUE)
  for (cl in de_cols) f$site_info[[cl]] <- strength * f0$site_info[[cl]]

  f$site_info$editing_sampling_model <- "beta_binomial"
  
  #phi controls how tight that variation is: higher phi = replicates more 
  #similar to each other, lower phi = noisier replicates.
  f$site_info$precision              <- phi
  
  #Every transcript gets the same expression (1000), and each site's depth 
  #is scaled by target_depth / 1000, so sites end up with roughly target_depth 
  #reads. This removes expression differences so depth is under your control.
  #coverage_fraction is set to match the multiplier
  f$transcript_info$baseline_expr    <- 1000
  f$site_info$site_depth_multiplier  <- target_depth / 1000
  f$site_info$coverage_fraction      <- f$site_info$site_depth_multiplier

  # R copies p when you modify it inside a function, so the global p is
  # left untouched. Safe.
  pp <- p
  pp$design$lib_condition_scale[] <- 1
  pp$design$lib_sdlog <- 0

  # ---- (b) simulate --------------------------------------------------
  sim <- a2i_simulate(pp,
                      transcript_info = f$transcript_info,
                      site_info       = f$site_info,
                      n_per_condition = c(WT_mock = n_reps,
                                          ADAR1KO_mock = n_reps),
                      seed = seed)
  counts <- a2i_refalt_counts(sim)

  # number of truly differential sites BEFORE filtering
  n_true_all <- sum(counts$site_info$editable &
                    counts$site_info$de_logit_shift_conditionADAR1KO_mock != 0)
  # ---- (c) filter ----------------------------------------------------
  #This finds which sample columns are WT (iA) and which are knockout (iB).
  cond <- as.character(counts$sample_info$condition)
  iA <- which(cond == "WT_mock"); iB <- which(cond == "ADAR1KO_mock")
  
  #Depth is total reads. A sample is "usable" at a site if it has at least 
  #10 reads, and "detected" if it's usable and has at least 2 edited reads 
  #(so a single stray read doesn't count as editing).
  dep <- counts$alt + counts$ref
  usable   <- dep >= 10
  detected <- usable & counts$alt >= 2

  #This is the editing proportion per sample (edited reads ÷ total reads). 
  #Where there are zero reads, it's set to NA instead of dividing by zero.
  pr_ <- counts$alt / dep; pr_[dep == 0] <- NA
  
  n_det_A <- rowSums(detected[, iA, drop = FALSE])
  n_det_B <- rowSums(detected[, iB, drop = FALSE])
  me_A <- rowSums(pr_[, iA, drop = FALSE] * usable[, iA, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE) /
          pmax(rowSums(usable[, iA, drop = FALSE]), 1)
  me_B <- rowSums(pr_[, iB, drop = FALSE] * usable[, iB, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE) /
          pmax(rowSums(usable[, iB, drop = FALSE]), 1)

  keep <- pmax(n_det_A, n_det_B) >= 2 & pmax(me_A, me_B) >= 0.10

  #This subsets everything to the kept sites and recomputes depth.
  alt <- counts$alt[keep, , drop = FALSE]
  ref <- counts$ref[keep, , drop = FALSE]
  si  <- counts$site_info[keep, , drop = FALSE]
  dep <- alt + ref

  #a site is truly differential if it's editable and the simulator gave it a 
  #nonzero shift in the knockout. grp is the group label for each sample, with 
  #WT set as the reference level.
  truth <- si$editable & si$de_logit_shift_conditionADAR1KO_mock != 0
  grp   <- factor(cond, levels = c("WT_mock", "ADAR1KO_mock"))

  # If a scenario has no true positives or no sites left,
  # bail out cleanly rather than crashing the whole loop.
  #if (nrow(alt) == 0) return(NULL)

  # ---- (d) the four tests -------------------------------------------
  #This converts each sample's editing proportion to the logit scale. 
  #Proportions are squeezed between 0 and 1, which makes t-tests behave badly; 
  #the logit stretches them onto an unbounded scale. 
  #The small eps stops log(0) from blowing up when a 
  #proportion is exactly 0 or 1.
  prop <- alt / dep; prop[dep == 0] <- NA
  eps <- 0.005
  #lgt <- log((prop + eps) / (1 - prop + eps))
  lgt <- log((alt + 0.5) / (ref + 0.5)); lgt[dep == 0] <- NA

  #Test 1, t-test on logit values. 
  #For each site (each row), it splits values into WT and KO, drops missing 
  #ones, requires at least 2 per group 
  #(you can't estimate variability from one value), returns p = 1 if all values 
  #are identical (no difference, and t.test would error), and otherwise runs 
  #a Welch t-test. This treats each replicate as one data point, so it respects 
  #biological variability but ignores how many reads each sample had.
  p_ttest <- apply(lgt, 1, function(v) {
  x <- v[iA]; y <- v[iB]
  x <- x[is.finite(x)]; y <- y[is.finite(y)]
  if (length(x) < 2 || length(y) < 2) return(NA_real_)
  if (stats::sd(c(x, y)) == 0) return(1)
  stats::t.test(x, y)$p.value
})

  #Test 2, Fisher's exact test on pooled reads. 
  #It adds up all edited and unedited reads across replicates within each group, 
  #builds a 2×2 table (edited/unedited × WT/KO), and tests it. If a row of the 
  #table is all zeros, the test is skipped. use_fisher = FALSE lets you turn it 
  #off because it can be slow. The important weakness: 
  #pooling treats all reads as independent, as if they came from one giant 
  #sample, so it ignores that replicates genuinely differ. 
  #That makes it overconfident.
  if (use_fisher) {
    a1 <- rowSums(alt[, iA, drop = FALSE]); r1 <- rowSums(ref[, iA, drop = FALSE])
    a2 <- rowSums(alt[, iB, drop = FALSE]); r2 <- rowSums(ref[, iB, drop = FALSE])
    p_fisher <- vapply(seq_along(a1), function(i) {
      m <- matrix(c(a1[i], a2[i], r1[i], r2[i]), nrow = 2)
      if (any(rowSums(m) == 0)) return(NA_real_)
      stats::fisher.test(m)$p.value
    }, numeric(1))
  } else p_fisher <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(alt))

  #A helper that fits a logistic regression (GLM) for one site: 
  #"edited vs unedited reads, explained by group." co[2, 4] is the p-value 
  #for the group effect (row 2 = the KO-vs-WT coefficient, column 4 = p-value). 
  #tryCatch means if the fit errors or even just warns, return NA instead of 
  #stopping.
#  fit_p <- function(a, r, fam) {
#  suppressWarnings(tryCatch({
#    m   <- stats::glm(cbind(a, r) ~ grp, family = fam)
#    tab <- anova(m, test = if (fam$family == "binomial") "LRT" else "F")
#    tab[2, ncol(tab)]                       # last column = p-value
#  }, error = function(e) NA_real_))
# }
  fit_p <- function(a, r, fam) {
  tryCatch({
    m <- suppressWarnings(stats::glm(cbind(a, r) ~ grp, family = fam))
    test <- if (identical(fam$family, "binomial")) "Chisq" else "F"
    a_tab <- stats::anova(m, test = test)
    if (nrow(a_tab) < 2) NA_real_ else a_tab[2, ncol(a_tab)]
  }, error = function(e) NA_real_)
}
  
  
#  fit_p <- function(a, r, fam) {
#    tryCatch({
#      m  <- stats::glm(cbind(a, r) ~ grp, family = fam)
#      co <- summary(m)$coefficients
#      if (nrow(co) < 2) NA_real_ else co[2, 4]
#    }, error = function(e) NA_real_, warning = function(w) NA_real_)
#  }
  
  #Tests 3 and 4. 
  #The same GLM with two families. The plain binomial assumes reads vary only 
  #by sampling chance, much like Fisher, so it's also overconfident. 
  #The quasibinomial estimates an extra "overdispersion" factor from the data, 
  #meaning it notices that replicates vary more than chance alone predicts and 
  #widens its uncertainty accordingly. vapply(..., numeric(1)) loops over sites 
  #and guarantees each result is a single number.
  p_binom <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(alt)),
                    function(i) fit_p(alt[i, ], ref[i, ], stats::binomial()),
                    numeric(1))
  p_quasi <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(alt)),
                    function(i) fit_p(alt[i, ], ref[i, ], stats::quasibinomial()),
                    numeric(1))

  # ---- (e) score, and tag every row with the settings used ----------
  # This tagging is the important bit: without it you cannot tell which
  # row came from which setting once everything is stacked together.
  out <- rbind(
    cbind(method = "t-test (logit)",    evaluate(p_ttest,  truth)),
    cbind(method = "Fisher (pooled)",   evaluate(p_fisher, truth)),
    cbind(method = "GLM binomial",      evaluate(p_binom,  truth)),
    cbind(method = "GLM quasibinomial", evaluate(p_quasi,  truth))
  )
  
  out$n_true_all <- n_true_all
  out$recall_overall <- out$TP / n_true_all 
  
  cbind(out,
        n_reps = n_reps, strength = strength,
        target_depth = target_depth, phi = phi, seed = seed,
        row.names = NULL)
}

# Try it once to check it works before looping.
run_one(seed = 102)
```


```{r rotate over parameters}
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Sweep ONE parameter, repeat over several seeds
#
# expand.grid builds every combination of the values you give it. Here:
# 4 replicate counts x 3 seeds = 12 runs. lapply walks the rows, and
# do.call(rbind, ...) stacks the 12 small tables into one big one.
#
# Three seeds is the minimum worth doing; 5-10 is better. One seed is a
# single roll of the dice and will mislead you.
# ------------------------------------------------------------------

grid_reps <- expand.grid(n_reps = c(3, 5, 8, 12),
                         seed   = 1:3)

sweep_reps <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(grid_reps)), function(i) {
  message("run ", i, " of ", nrow(grid_reps))   # progress, this is slow
  run_one(n_reps = grid_reps$n_reps[i],
          seed   = grid_reps$seed[i])
  # everything else stays at the defaults written in run_one():
  # strength = 1, target_depth = 100, phi = 50
}))

head(sweep_reps)
```


```{r}
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Average over seeds
#
# You have 3 rows per (n_reps, method) - one per seed. Collapse them to
# one mean, so the lines are steady instead of jagged.
# aggregate() = "for each combination of method and n_reps, average these
# columns".
# ------------------------------------------------------------------

avg_reps <- aggregate(cbind(balanced_accuracy, AUC, AUPRC, AUPRC_baseline, precision, recall) ~ method + n_reps,
                      data = sweep_reps, FUN = mean, na.rm = TRUE,
                      na.action = na.pass)
base_reps <- aggregate(AUPRC_baseline ~ n_reps, data = avg_reps, FUN = mean)

#avg_reps
```


```{r TNTPFNTN_rep plot}

avg_reps_calls <- aggregate(cbind(TP, TN, FN, FP) ~ method + n_reps,
                      data = sweep_reps, FUN = mean, na.rm = TRUE,
                      na.action = na.pass)

metrics <- c("TP", "TN", "FN", "FP")
reps_calls <- do.call(rbind, lapply(metrics, function(mm) {
  data.frame(method = avg_reps_calls$method,
             n_reps = avg_reps_calls$n_reps,
             metric = mm,
             value  = avg_reps_calls[[mm]])
}))
# fix the panel order so precision and recall sit next to each other
reps_calls$metric <- factor(reps_calls$metric,
                           levels = c("TP", "TN", "FN", "FP"))

calls_reps <- ggplot(reps_calls, aes(method, value, fill = metric)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  facet_wrap(~ n_reps, labeller = label_both) +
  labs(title = "Calls per test (n_reps sweep)",
       subtitle = "strength = 1, depth = 100, phi = 50; mean of 3 seeds",
       x = NULL, y = "number of sites", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))

#ggsave("calls_reps.png",  calls_reps,  width = 6,  height = 4.5, dpi = 150)
```

```{r plot n_reps, eval=FALSE, include=FALSE}
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. PLOT
#
# ggplot wants LONG format: one row per point to be drawn, with a column
# saying which metric it is. Right now accuracy/AUC/precision/recall are
# four separate columns (wide format), so reshape first.
#
# After reshaping:
#   x      = n_reps      (the thing you varied)
#   y      = value       (the metric)
#   colour = method      (one line per test)
#   facet  = metric      (one small panel per metric)
# ------------------------------------------------------------------

# base-R way to go wide -> long: stack the four metric columns on top of
# each other and keep a label saying which was which.
metrics <- c("balanced_accuracy", "AUC", "precision", "recall")
long_reps <- do.call(rbind, lapply(metrics, function(mm) {
  data.frame(method = avg_reps$method,
             n_reps = avg_reps$n_reps,
             metric = mm,
             value  = avg_reps[[mm]])
}))
# fix the panel order so precision and recall sit next to each other
long_reps$metric <- factor(long_reps$metric,
                           levels = c("recall", "precision", "AUC", "balanced_accuracy"))

ggplot(long_reps, aes(n_reps, value, colour = method)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  facet_wrap(~metric) +          # four small plots sharing one legend
  ylim(0, 1) +
  labs(title = "Effect of replicate number on each test",
       subtitle = "strength = 1, depth = 100, phi = 50; mean of 3 seeds",
       x = "replicates per condition", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

# WHAT TO LOOK FOR
#  - the recall panel is the power curve. Fisher's line should be nearly
#    flat: it pools reads and never sees replicates, so more replicates
#    do not help it in the way they help the others.
#  - the precision panel is the check. A line that sits below 0.95 is a
#    method whose FDR control has failed. Fisher and binomial GLM should
#    sit low; quasibinomial should hug 0.95.
#  - read the two together. High recall on the Fisher line means nothing
#    if its precision panel shows it was guessing.
```


```{r}
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. The same thing for the other three knobs
#
# Identical pattern - only the swept column changes. The parameters you
# are NOT sweeping simply are not passed, so run_one() uses its defaults.
# ------------------------------------------------------------------

# a small helper so you do not repeat yourself
sweep_over <- function(param, values, seeds = 1:3) {
  g <- expand.grid(value = values, seed = seeds)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(g)), function(i) {
    args <- list(seed = g$seed[i])
    args[[param]] <- g$value[i]          # set only the swept parameter
    do.call(run_one, args)
  }))
}


# and plot with the same three steps: aggregate -> reshape long -> ggplot,
# swapping `n_reps` for `strength` / `target_depth` / `phi`.

# NOTE on strength = 0: there are no true positives, so recall and
# precision are undefined (NA) and only the false positive count is
# meaningful. Report that run separately as a null check - "how many
# sites did each method call when nothing was different" - rather than
# as a point on the power curve.
```

```{r target_depth, eval=FALSE, include=FALSE}
# 1. run the sweep (strength, phi, n_reps stay at run_one() defaults)
sweep_depth <- sweep_over("target_depth", c(20, 50, 100, 500))

# 2. average over seeds
avg_depth <- aggregate(cbind(balanced_accuracy, AUC, precision, recall) ~ method + target_depth,
                       data = sweep_depth, FUN = mean, na.rm = TRUE,
                       na.action = na.pass)

# 3. wide -> long
metrics <- c("balanced_accuracy", "AUC", "precision", "recall")
long_depth <- do.call(rbind, lapply(metrics, function(mm) {
  data.frame(method       = avg_depth$method,
             target_depth = avg_depth$target_depth,
             metric       = mm,
             value        = avg_depth[[mm]])
}))
long_depth$metric <- factor(long_depth$metric,
                            levels = c("recall", "precision", "AUC", "balanced_accuracy"))

# 4. plot
ggplot(long_depth, aes(target_depth, value, colour = method)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  facet_wrap(~metric) +
  scale_x_log10() +              # 20, 50, 100, 500 spread out evenly
  ylim(0, 1) +
  labs(title = "Effect of sequencing depth on each test",
       subtitle = "n_reps = 3, strength = 1, phi = 50; mean of 3 seeds",
       x = "target depth", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

```{r}
# a small helper so you do not repeat yourself
sweep_over_2 <- function(param, values, seeds = 1:3, n_reps = 8) {
  g <- expand.grid(value = values, seed = seeds)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(g)), function(i) {
   args <- list(seed = g$seed[i], n_reps = n_reps)
   args[[param]] <- g$value[i]
   do.call(run_one, args)
  }))
}
```
